chunks: My father, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

Those before us say: When Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, loves a servant, He announces it from the heavens, saying 'Allah loves so-and-so, so love him,' and love is cast into the hearts of the people for him. And when Allah hates a servant, He announces it from the heavens, saying 'Allah hates so-and-so, so hate him,' and He says: Allah casts hatred into the hearts of the people for him.

He (peace be upon him) was reclining, then sat up straight and shook his hand three times, saying: No, it is not as they say. But when Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, loves a servant, He incites the people on earth against him so they speak ill of him, thereby incurring sin for themselves and earning reward for him. And when Allah hates a servant, He makes him beloved to the people so they speak ill of him, thereby incurring sin for themselves and incurring sin for him.

Then he (peace be upon him) said: Who was more beloved to Allah than Yahya ibn Zakariya (peace be upon him)? They were incited against him until they killed him. And who was more beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, than Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him)? He received from the people what you already know. And who was more beloved to Allah, the Exalted, than Al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him)? They were incited against him until they killed him.
ai.seo_question: How does divine love or hatred affect human perception and sin according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this rare meaning (ma'ani al-akhbar) where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) corrects the prevalent notion of 'divine love leading to human affection' by introducing the concept of 'fitnah through elevation.' He explains that divine love often manifests as increased scrutiny and hostility from the masses, a test that yields greater reward for the beloved servant, as exemplified by the martyrdoms of Yahya, Ali, and Al-Husayn (AS). This highlights the Shia theological perspective that true spiritual status is often concealed or tested through external opposition rather than popular acclaim.
